Oversight
OH-ver-syte
n.
From over and sight. Webster 1828 gives two nearly opposite senses: superintendence, watchful care; and an overlooking, an omission or mistake. The English word thus contains both the elder’s duty and the failure of it, which is a small accident of language worth noticing.

Biblical Definition

Oversight is Peter’s word for the eldership, and the verse in which it stands is the fullest job description of the office in Scripture: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind (1 Peter 5:2). Three contrasts, and each names a real temptation — the man who serves because he cannot get out of it, the man who serves for money, and the man who serves to be somebody, addressed in the next verse as neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. The Greek verb is the one behind bishop, which is why the New Testament uses elder, bishop, overseer, and pastor of a single office; Peter, writing as a fellow elder, uses the shepherd word and the overseer word in the same sentence. Paul does the same at Miletus, calling for the elders of Ephesus and telling them the Holy Ghost has made them overseers, to feed the church of God which He purchased with His own blood. The Old Testament uses the word of the men set over the temple work — the Levites who had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OVERSIGHT as superintendence, watchful care, as of an overseer; and also a mistake, an omission, an inadvertency — the two senses arising from the two ways one may look over a thing.

expand to see more

OVERSIGHT, n. — Superintendence; watchful care; as, the oversight of a school or of a flock.

Mistake; error; omission; an overlooking; as, this fault was an oversight.

OVERSEER, n. — One who overlooks; a superintendent; and in Scripture, a bishop or elder (Acts 20:28).

The double sense arises from the two ways of looking over a thing — watching it, or passing over it without seeing.

The New Testament uses episkopos, overseer or bishop, and presbuteros, elder, of the same men (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5, 7).

Key Scripture

1 Peter 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Acts 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Titus 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Titus 1:7 — "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;"

Hebrews 13:17 — "Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you."

Modern Corruption

The identification of elder, bishop, and overseer as one office is the plainest exegetical ground of Presbyterian and congregational polity against the threefold hierarchy, and Titus 1:5-7 makes the interchange within two verses.

expand to see more

Paul tells Titus to ordain elders in every city, and then two verses later gives the qualifications for a bishop, describing the same men. At Miletus he summons the elders of the church and tells them the Holy Ghost has made them overseers and charges them to feed — that is, to pastor — the flock. Peter, calling himself an elder, does the same in one verse. Three terms, one office, and no trace in the New Testament of a bishop set over a college of presbyters. The later development of the monarchical episcopate, and the Roman papacy built upon it, are not found in the apostolic writings, and this is why the Reformed churches restored a plurality of elders in each congregation.

The polity argument matters less pastorally than the three temptations Peter names, which the office attracts in every generation. Not by constraint, but willingly — against the man serving out of guilt or because nobody else would, whose ministry becomes an endurance. Not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind — against the man for whom it is a living, a caution Paul repeats to Timothy and Titus, and one that the modern celebrity ministry with its book deals and conference fees should read slowly. And neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock — against the domineering elder, whose sin our Lord addressed by washing feet. Hebrews adds the flock’s side: they watch for your souls and must give account, so let them do it with joy.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek episkopeo (G1983), to oversee, to look upon, at 1 Peter 5:2; episkopos (G1985), an overseer or bishop; presbuteros (G4245), an elder; poimaino (G4165), to shepherd.

expand to see more

Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, to take the oversight; 1 Peter 5:2 and Hebrews 12:15.

Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, bishop; Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:7.

Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder; used of the same men at Acts 20:17 and Titus 1:5.

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd, to feed; feed the flock of God (1 Peter 5:2).

Hebrew peqiddah and melakah — the Levites who had the oversight of the outward business of the house of God (Nehemiah 11:16).

Usage

"Taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly (1 Peter 5:2) — the office and its first temptation."

"The Holy Ghost hath made you overseers (Acts 20:28) — elders, overseers, and shepherds as one office."

"They watch for your souls, as they that must give account (Hebrews 13:17) — the weight the oversight carries."
